title: Gaitskill Mound's engraved tablets
summary: On Mount Sterling's northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it…
bodyMarkdown:
Beside Mount Sterling's northern bypass (KY 686) in Kentucky stands Gaitskill Mound, an earthwork far older than the town. The [Kentucky Historical Society marker for the Gaitskill Mound](https://history.ky.gov/markers/the-gaitskill-mound) (No. 1655) identifies it as an Indian mound built by Adena people. The marker gives their time in the Ohio Valley as about 800 B.C. to A.D. 700. The mound was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.

## The Adena people

The marker describes the Adena as people who began cultivating simple crops, which created a mixed economy of hunting and farming. "Central to Adena life," it says, "were rituals involving cremation and mound building."

Other sources draw the Adena era differently. [Grokipedia's Adena culture article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) dates the culture to about 600 BCE to 100 CE and notes that chronologies vary by region and source. It describes small, mobile communities in the central and upper Ohio Valley that supplemented hunting and gathering with crops such as goosefoot, sunflower and squash.

Their best-known works are conical burial mounds and circular earthworks that served as ceremonial centers. In Kentucky's Bluegrass region, Adena sites show shared ritual practices.

## How the tablets told the story

According to the marker, engraved stone tablets found at the Gaitskill Mound show that it is an Adena mound. The marker does not say when the tablets were found, who found them or where they are now.

The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Wright-Mounds.aspx) explains why such tablets are telling. Adena people carved palm-sized rectangular tablets from shale, limestone, siltstone or fine sandstone. They engraved them with distinctive designs, often highly stylized wild turkeys or birds of prey. The survey says the designs may reflect a layered universe, with the earth suspended between a sky world and a watery underworld.

Only four such tablets are known from Kentucky's Adena sites. Just one of them, from the [Wright Mounds](/stories/wright-mounds-montgomery-county/) elsewhere in Montgomery County, was found by archaeologists during an excavation.

What the tablets were used for is still debated. [Wikipedia](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture) notes that paint has been found on some Adena tablets. That has led archaeologists to propose that they were used to stamp designs on cloth, hides or skin, possibly as outlines for tattoos.

## Kentucky today

Montgomery County's Adena heritage shaped the name of its county seat. [Grokipedia's Mount Sterling article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mount_Sterling,_Kentucky) describes another large Adena mound, about 25 feet high and 125 feet across, at what is now Queen and Locust streets. It held artifacts such as shell necklaces and copper beads. The settlement was first called Little Mountain Town after that mound.

It was established in 1792 and took its permanent name from Stirling, the Scottish hometown of founder Hugh Forbes. For another Adena site in northeastern Kentucky, see [Ashland's Adena mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/).
